blindSummary:
This country combines a conservative political climate and significant legal-protection gaps for trans people with a landmark supranational-court ruling and active civil society that give some positive trajectory. The top court of the supranational union this country belongs to ruled in 2024 that it must recognise gender-identity changes made in other member states (a landmark individual case), and a national court definitively confirmed this in March 2026. The capital's Pride marked its 20th anniversary with tens of thousands of marchers.

However, domestic legal gender recognition is court-based, restrictive, and inconsistently implemented. The anti-discrimination law does not explicitly cover gender identity (it covers "sex" and "sexual orientation" only), and the hate-crime law's aggravating-circumstance provision has never been applied in SOGIESC cases. No same-sex marriage or civil unions are recognised (the country's dominant church successfully opposed reform). Far-right influences rose during the 2024-2025 election cycle, with anti-LGBTI rhetoric "intensified and repeatedly instrumentalised for political mobilisation."

For a visitor: union membership with passport-free travel to neighbours, no trans-specific border friction, no criminalisation, bathrooms unrestricted. The union-court ruling means legal-gender-recognition documents issued by member states must be recognised.
blindOutOfScope: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is moderate.
blindSourceSummaries: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying international news-agency report (Oct 2024) covers the union-court ruling that this country infringed a transgender man's rights - the case concerned a gender recognition obtained in another member state.

LGBT-rights organisation case update (March 2026): definitive victory in a strategic applicant's case - a court in one of the capital's districts ruled (now final after appeals were rejected) that the state must issue the applicant a new birth certificate reflecting the gender identity already recognised in another member state before that state's withdrawal from the union, following the 2024 union-court ruling establishing the obligation.

Regional LGBTI-rights organisation annual review 2026 (covering 2025), chapter on this country: anti-LGBTI rhetoric intensified during the presidential campaign (one nationalist candidate campaigned 'against LGBTQ'; the prime minister made 'skirt' remarks); an LGBT-rights organisation's complaint led to a public warning to a commercial broadcaster for defamatory Pride coverage; a far-right deputy mayor of one city vowed never to allow an LGBTI event there; misinformation followed the union's LGBTI equality strategy 2026-2030.

The same regional body's annual review 2024 (covering 2023), chapter on this country: the national anti-discrimination authority investigated printing houses refusing LGBT-related print jobs; one legislator blamed LGBTQI people for bad weather as divine punishment; 51% of the public agree same-sex families should have legal recognition (2023 polling survey); new education-law proposals included diversity obligations, opposed by 13 religious groups; a new fiscal code threatens associations' ability to distribute services.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): anti-discrimination ordinance since 2000 but limited institutional progress; no same-sex marriage/civil unions (the dominant church a key opponent; a 2018 referendum failed on turnout); a regional human-rights court ruled in May 2023 that this country's ban on same-sex unions violates the private-life article of the regional convention, but the government has defied the ruling; legal gender change possible but inaccessible, inconsistent and requiring surgical intervention.

Regional inter-governmental body's thematic review (Jan 2023): hate crimes and other hate-motivated incidents against LGBTI people in this country - a national report on implementation of the body's anti-discrimination recommendation, covering legal/policy frameworks, applicable regional human-rights court case-law and international standards.

The regional LGBTI-rights organisation and partner organisations' submission to the union's 2025 rule-of-law report - a targeted stakeholder consultation covering horizontal developments and country chapters across several member states.
A newswire report (Jun 2025): tens of thousands join this country's capital pride march on its 20th anniversary, against rising right-wing hostility toward the LGBTQ+ community.

The union fundamental-rights agency's legal study (Feb 2008) by two local researchers: legal study on homophobia and discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation in this country - implementation of the union's employment-equality directive, the national anti-discrimination body's work, freedom of movement, asylum, family reunification, and freedom of assembly including cases of refusals or bans.
blindLocalsOnly: The court-based domestic legal-gender-recognition regime and its inconsistent implementation are resident-facing; the union-court ruling directly benefits trans visitors with member-state-issued recognition documents.
blindTangential: No same-sex marriage or civil unions recognised — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
